notes.meaning: The poem's speaker steps forward as a man who has lived through deep trouble. Some older teachers think this is Jeremiah speaking of his own suffering. Others think he speaks for all of God's people, or for the godly who suffered when Jerusalem fell. The "rod" is God's, used to correct and not to destroy. Even though God is not named, the speaker knows his pain comes from God's just anger.

differ.view: Some see this suffering man as a picture pointing ahead to Christ, the "Man of sorrows," who was struck by God's justice in our place.
Methodist commentary has held that there is no real basis for reading these lines as being about Christ's sufferings. They describe the prophet or his people.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: The Hebrew word for "man" can suggest a beaten soldier or an "everyman" figure. He can stand for any member of the community, man or woman.

notes.meaning: In the Bible, darkness often stands for trouble and light for good times. God has led him into the darkness he feared, not the light he hoped for. Even God's own people sometimes walk in darkness.

God seems to have turned against him like an enemy. The hand that once protected him now strikes him again and again, all day long, without a break. When God's hand keeps striking, it is tempting to think His heart has turned against us too.

His grief has worn him out so much that he looks old. All his beauty and strength are gone. "Broken bones" is a picture of a crushed spirit and lost strength. Nothing is more dreadful than feeling that God is angry with us.

He uses the picture of a city under siege. God has built siege walls around him so that he cannot get out. He is surrounded by bitterness, as bitter as poison, and by weary hardship. This may also recall the earth mounds the Babylonians built to take Jerusalem.

His darkness feels like the darkness of the grave. He is like people long dead and forgotten, with no hope of coming back. The words sound extreme, but no words can fully express the sorrow of believers who feel God's anger.

He feels like a prisoner shut into a small space with no way out. On top of that, his chains are so heavy he can hardly move his feet. The chains may have been made of bronze. He has looked for a way of escape and found none.

Worst of all, his loud and earnest prayers seem to go nowhere, as if God has shut the door on them. God never truly rejects His own people. But He sometimes holds back His answer to test their patience. Then they may feel unheard. This is meant to move them to keep praying harder and more often.

God has blocked his way with a wall of cut stone, too strong to break through. His paths are made crooked, so his plans for safety all fail. This does not mean God leads people into wrong unfairly. It means every plan he made came to nothing.

God seems like a bear or lion hiding in ambush, ready to pounce. The speaker could never feel safe. He feels dragged off the road, torn apart and left alone. These are harsh words about God. Believers in deep pain sometimes say more than is right, and their words show how weak even the strongest can be.
Now God is pictured as an archer, and the speaker is His target. The arrows are the troubles God sends. They pierce his "kidneys," meaning his deepest inner parts. No part of him is left untouched.

On top of his pain, people laugh at him and make up mocking songs about him. The mockers seem to be the scoffers among his own people, who ignored the prophets' warnings. Mockery makes sorrow far more bitter.

Wormwood is a very bitter plant. It stands for great trouble and sorrow. He has had so much bitterness that he feels drunk on it, unable to think straight. Even faithful believers feel this. The answer is to bring that bitterness to God rather than feed it.

His life is like bread full of grit that breaks the teeth. Some think of bread baked in ashes. Others see a picture of cruel treatment. He has also been pressed down into the dust and ashes, a sign of deep sorrow and shame. Mourners used to put ashes on their heads.
All peace is gone from him. To the Hebrews, peace meant every kind of well-being. Good times feel so far away that he has forgotten what they were like. Everywhere he looks, he sees no hope.

Here his complaint hits bottom. He thinks his strength is gone and he has nothing left to hope for from the LORD. Even believers can feel this kind of near-despair, but they should not give in to it. It is also the turning point. For the first time he speaks God's name, and that name, the God who keeps His promises, holds him back from despair.

He sums up all his pain: the trouble, the wandering, the wormwood and the gall (two bitter things that picture great suffering). Many read this as a prayer asking God to "remember" his trouble. Others take it as the speaker still thinking about his troubles, which explains why he nearly lost hope.

He cannot stop thinking about his troubles, and they press his soul down low. That humbling also leads him to sorrow for sin. As he humbles himself under God's hand, his hope begins to come back. Believers should face their troubles honestly, but not dwell on them until despair takes over.

Now the tone changes. He brings something back to mind, and because of it, he has hope. The "this" points ahead to what he says next about God's nature and care. Without hope the heart would break. God brings light out of darkness.

Here is what gives him hope. Bad as things are, it is only because of the LORD's loving devotion (His faithful, promise-keeping love) that His people have not been wiped out. Given our sins, things could have been far worse. God's mercies never run dry, even when He seems angry. For His promise's sake, He will always keep His people.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some versions and scholars follow a slightly different Hebrew reading. It says "the LORD's loving devotion never ceases," not "we are not consumed," because that matches the next line better.
